candidate_payload.early_body_text: doi: 10. 1093/brain/awy095 brain 2018: 141; 1–2 | e49 letter to the editor atad1 encephalopathy and stiff baby syndrome: a recognizable clinical presentation 1 department of child neurology and amsterdam neuroscience, vu university medical center, amsterdam, the netherlands 2 division of human genetics, medical university innsbruck, innsbruck, austria 3 department of clinical chemistry, vu medical center, amsterdam, the netherlands 4 pediatric neurology, university children’s hospital, heidelberg, germany 5 pediatric neurology and metabolic medicine, center for pediatric and adolescent medicine, and center for rare disorders, heidelberg university hospital, heidelberg, germany correspondence to: nicole i. wolf deptartment of child neurology vu university medical center de boelelaan 1118 1081 hv amsterdam the netherlands e-mail: n.wolf@vumc.nl sir, a recent study published in brain described the second family with a homozygous mutation in atad1, leading to a lethal encephalopathy (piard et al., 2018). during the past decade, advances in genetic testing have completely changed diagnostic approach and success rate in patients with rare neurological disorders, especially in those with normal imaging and metabolic studies. still, when a genetic variant in a highly consanguineous family is identified without another, independent patient confirming that mutations in this gene are indeed disease causing, association with disease may remain uncertain, even when clinical and functional data are compelling (warman chardon et al., 2015). this was the case in an elegant study by ahrens-nicklas et al. (2017), describing a consanguineous family with several affected children all found to carry a homozygous variant in atad1. the patients they analysed were symptomatic at birth with extreme hypertonia and non-responsive to stimuli, later severe brain atrophy and finally early death. the second report by piard et al. (2018) confirmed the findings of the first publication and added more functional data on pathophysiology (piard et al., 2018). we would like to add a third family we saw more than 25 years ago and diagnosed last year, thanks to the detailed description of the first atad1 family. the female patient was born in 1992 at 37 + 5 weeks gestational age by caesarean section because of pathological ctg and premature rupture of membranes. parents were consanguineous, and family history was uneventful. apgar scores were 8, 9 and 10, birth weight 2420 g, length and head circumference 32. 5 cm (below 2 sd). directly postpartum, muscle tone was severely elevated with flexion of arms and legs, closed fists and myoclonic jerks amplified by the slightest physical stimulus although the child did not react to sounds. muscle tendon reflexes were exaggerated. she did not show spontaneous movements. muscle tone improved a little during sleep. she was able to feed from a bottle, albeit with difficulties. first metabolic investigations (glucose and ammoniac) were normal as well as routine laboratory parameters and brain ultrasound. at the age of almost 4 months, she was able to fixate and smile in spite of absent motor development. rigidity increased until it persisted also during sleep. oral baclofen, phenobarbital and diazepam had no effect on the clinical symptoms. attacks of hypoxia developed which were not attributable to epilepsy, and the child died at age 8 months advance access publication april 12, 2018 ß the author(s) (2018). published by oxford university press on behalf of the guarantors of brain. all rights reserved. for permissions, please email: journals.permissions@oup.com nicole i. wolf, 1 johannes zschocke, 2 cornelis jakobs, 3 dietz rating4 and georg f. hoffmann5 e49 | brain 2018: 141; 1–2 gad antibodies. the genetic basis of this disorder could not be proven back then, neither were there specific therapeutic options besides vigabatrin. perampanel, which is an ampa receptor inhibitor (zaccara et al., 2013), had a positive effect on muscle tone and seizures in the index patients (ahrens-nicklas et al., 2017), but was not available in 1992. our case also illustrates the power of meticulous clinical case descriptions including video material, certainly for rare neurological disorders. the main finding of an extremely stiff infant without spontaneous movements, resembling a wooden doll, also described by piard and colleagues, should suggest atad1 deficiency and ensue a therapeutic trial with perampanel, even before genetic confirmation. funding no funding was received towards this work. references ahrens-nicklas r, umanah g, sondheimer n, deardorff ma, wilkens ab, conlin lk, et al. precision therapy for a new disorder of ampa receptor recycling due to mutations in atad1. neurol genet. 2017; 3: e130. hoffmann gf, jakobs c, meinck h-m, rating d. stiff-baby-like syndrome with severely diminished gaba in csf—a defect of glutamic acid decarboxylase? ped res 1994; 35: 266. piard j, essien umanah gk, harms fl, abalde-atristain
